entries.description: Turns a raw meeting transcript or a handful of jotted lines into structured notes: decisions, action items with owners, and open questions.
entries.name: Meeting Notes
entries.skill_body:
---
name: meeting-notes
description: Turn raw meeting transcripts or jotted lines into structured notes with decisions, action items and open questions.
version: 1.0.0
---

# Meeting Notes

When the user shares a meeting transcript, a recording summary, or rough
notes from a meeting, produce structured notes in this shape:

## Decisions
- One line per decision, with who decided when it is known.

## Action items
- [ ] Action — Owner (due date if mentioned)

## Open questions
- Anything unresolved or ambiguous.

Rules:
- Keep it tight: no filler, no repeating the transcript back.
- If owners are unclear, write "Owner: ?" rather than guessing.
- Ask at most one clarifying question when the input is too thin to be useful.

entries.author: community
entries.description: A careful second pair of eyes for a diff or a pasted snippet: correctness bugs first, then edge cases, then style — with file and line references.
entries.name: Code Reviewer
entries.skill_body:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Review a diff or pasted code for correctness bugs, edge cases and style, with file and line references.
version: 1.0.0
---

# Code Reviewer

When the user asks for a code review (a diff, a file, or a pasted snippet):

1. **Correctness first** — logic bugs, off-by-ones, null handling, error paths,
   concurrency hazards. Quote the exact lines.
2. **Edge cases** — empty inputs, huge inputs, failure modes of dependencies.
3. **Style last** — only flag what genuinely hurts readability or maintenance.

Format findings as: severity (blocker / suggestion), file:line, what is wrong,
and a concrete fix. End with a one-line verdict: ship it, fix-then-ship, or
needs rework. Never rewrite the whole file unasked — show the smallest diff
that fixes each blocker.

entries.name: Fetch
PDF Reader
entries.description: Extracts text from PDF files so the agent can summarize, search and quote documents.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: pdf-reader
description: Extract text from PDF files for summarizing, searching and quoting.
---

# PDF Reader

When the user points at a PDF (or you find one in the workspace), extract its
text before trying to answer questions about it.

## How to read a PDF

1. Prefer `pdftotext` when available:
   `pdftotext /path/to/file.pdf - | head -c 60000`
2. Fallback: `python3 -c "import pypdf; r=pypdf.PdfReader('/path/to/file.pdf'); print('\n'.join(p.extract_text() or '' for p in r.pages))"`
3. For scanned/image PDFs with no text layer, say so honestly and offer to
   read specific pages as images with read_image instead of guessing.

## Rules

- Never invent page numbers or quotes. Quote verbatim or say the text was
  unclear.
- For long documents, extract in chunks and summarize section by section.
- If the PDF is password-protected, ask the user for the password — never
  try to crack it.

entries.name: YouTube Summarizer
entries.description: Summarizes YouTube videos from transcripts: key points, timestamps, takeaways.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: youtube-summarizer
description: Summarize a YouTube video from its transcript with key points and timestamps.
---

# YouTube Summarizer

When the user shares a YouTube link and wants the gist, fetch the transcript
and summarize — don't make them watch 20 minutes.

## Steps

1. Try `yt-dlp --skip-download --write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --convert-subs srt -o /tmp/subs '%(id)s.%(ext)s' <url>` then read the .srt.
2. If subtitles are unavailable, use browser_use to open the video page and
   read the description/chapters, and say the summary is partial.
3. Produce: one-line verdict, 5-8 key points with timestamps where known,
   and any action items or links mentioned.

## Rules

- Never invent timestamps. If the transcript has none, say so.
- Keep it tight: the user wants the 2-minute version, not a retelling.

entries.name: Email Drafter
entries.description: Drafts clear, well-structured emails from a few rough lines. Pairs with the Gmail connector.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: email-drafter
description: Turn rough notes into a clear, well-structured email draft.
---

# Email Drafter

Turn the user's rough lines into an email that reads like they meant it.

## Process

1. Ask (or infer from context): recipient, purpose, tone (formal / friendly /
   firm), and any deadline.
2. Draft with: clear subject line, greeting, 2-4 short paragraphs, explicit
   ask or next step, sign-off.
3. Show the FULL draft and wait for approval before sending anything —
   never send email on a first draft without the user saying send.

## Rules

- Match the user's language (if they write in Hinglish, keep the flavor
  professional, not stiff).
- One ask per email. If they ramble about three topics, suggest splitting.
- If the Gmail connector is available, offer to send via gmail_send only
  after explicit approval.

entries.name: Travel Planner
entries.description: Builds day-by-day trip itineraries from a destination, dates and budget.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: travel-planner
description: Build day-by-day trip itineraries from destination, dates and budget.
---

# Travel Planner

Turn "I want to go to X" into a day-by-day plan the user can actually follow.

## Process

1. Collect: destination, dates (or duration), budget level (budget / mid /
   comfortable), interests (food, nature, history, shopping), pace
   (packed / relaxed).
2. Research current practicalities with web search or browser_use: visa
   needs, weather for the dates, rough prices.
3. Deliver: overview + cost estimate, then Day 1..N with morning / afternoon /
   evening blocks, food picks, and one backup option per day for bad weather.

## Rules

- Prices are estimates — say so, and never state a fare as fact without a
  source.
- Flag visa / entry requirements early; they're the most-forgotten item.
- Keep travel days realistic: no 6-attraction days.

entries.name: Code Explainer
entries.description: Explains code in plain language: what it does, why, and where the traps are.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: code-explainer
description: Explain what code does in plain language, with the traps highlighted.
---

# Code Explainer

When the user pastes code (or points at a file) and asks what it does:

1. Read the code first with file_read — never explain from memory of the
   filename.
2. Explain in layers: one-sentence summary, then what each important part
   does, then the traps (edge cases, hidden assumptions, things that break).
3. Match their level: if they say they're new, avoid jargon or define it
   inline. If they're experienced, skip the basics.

## Rules

- If the code has a bug and they didn't ask for review, mention it briefly
  once — don't turn an explanation into an unsolicited audit.
- Use small snippets to illustrate, not walls of code.

entries.name: Git Helper
entries.description: Git workflows done right: commits, branches, rebases, and undoing mistakes.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: git-helper
description: Git workflows done right — commits, branches, rebases, undoing mistakes.
---

# Git Helper

The user has zero git knowledge; be the careful senior dev they don't have.

## Rules

- NEVER force-push, hard-reset, or rewrite history without spelling out
  exactly what will be lost and getting explicit approval.
- Commit messages: short imperative summary + what/why in the body.
- Before any destructive command, show the command and what it does, then
  wait for a yes.
- Prefer safe undo paths: `git revert` over `reset --hard` for shared
  branches; stash before switching branches with dirty work.

## Useful flows

- New work: branch from main, small commits, push, open PR.
- Messed up a commit message: `git commit --amend` (unpushed only).
- Find when a bug appeared: `git bisect`.

entries.name: Data Analyst
entries.description: Analyzes CSVs and spreadsheets with Python: summaries, trends, charts.
entries.author: community
entries.skill_body:
---
name: data-analyst
description: Analyze CSVs and spreadsheets with Python — summaries, trends, charts.
---

# Data Analyst

When the user hands over a CSV/Excel file and wants answers:

1. Inspect first: `python3 -c "import pandas as pd; df=pd.read_csv('f'); print(df.shape); print(df.dtypes); print(df.head())"`.
2. Clean defensively: report missing values and odd types before analyzing;
   never silently drop rows that change the answer.
3. Answer their actual question, then add ONE interesting finding they
   didn't ask about.

## Rules

- Show the code you ran (or save it as a .py file) so the analysis is
  reproducible.
- Charts: save as PNG and share the file; describe the takeaway in words.
- Say "the data doesn't support that conclusion" when it doesn't — never
  torture numbers into a story.
